podcast.title: Initial Public Reaction and Intent
podcast.body: Upon the release of The Darkness's debut album *Permission to Land* in 2003, there was an initial public reaction questioning if the band, and Justin Hawkins's vocal style, was a joke or a parody of Freddie Mercury and Queen. However, Hawkins maintained that his approach was, and remains, entirely serious. His use of high-pitched vocals was noteworthy because it had been a long time since such a style was prevalent in Alt Rock. "This guy's making fun of Freddie Mercury or Queen. No, Justin was and remains dead serious."

podcast.title: Swimming Pool Chemical Burn Accident
podcast.body: Justin Vockins, the frontman of The Darkness, required emergency surgery due to injuries sustained in a bizarre swimming pool accident. While mixing chemicals for his pool, treated water burst out of the pump, causing his swimming shorts to melt onto his legs and resulting in chemical burns that necessitated surgical removal of the shorts and burns. "Justin Vockins, the frontman of the darkness, also required emergency surgery this past year for injuries resulting from a bizarre swimming pool accident."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Vocal Technique and Range
podcast.body: Justin Hawkins is known for his distinctive vocal style, often mistaken by journalists for falsetto. However, Hawkins clarifies that he primarily uses "head voice" for softer high singing and "high belt" for most of his powerful high notes, feeling the tone resonate in his head rather than throat or chest. He possesses an impressive vocal range of over four octaves, capable of reaching a low A (A2) and as high as an E6. "Justin says he doesn't use a falsetto. I quote, I use head voice for softer high singing, but it's mostly high belt."

podcast.title: Vocal Technique and Range
podcast.body: Justin Hawkins achieves his high notes by utilizing "head voice" for softer high singing and a "high belt" technique for more powerful passages, distinguishing his method from what journalists often incorrectly label as falsetto. He boasts an impressive vocal range spanning over four octaves, from a low A (A2) to a high E6. "I use head voice for softer high singing but it's mostly high belt. Journalists call it falsetto but that is mostly incorrect."
